**1\. Game Overview and Core Concept**

| *Submission Instructions: Provide a narrative describing your game. Explain how your game show adapts the rules of the classic 'Are You Smarter Than a 5th Grader?' TV program. Clearly state your game's unique theme, its elements, and how characters or roles are configured.* |
| :---- |

## **1.1 Game Description and Narrative Theme** {#1.1-game-description-and-narrative-theme}

ParadigmLocked recreates the popular "Are You Smarter Than a 5th Grader?" format as a programming paradigms learning tool. Inspired by Valve’s Deadlock, the game will be set inside a place called “Paradigm Space,” which mimics an abstract computational realm where programming paradigms manifest as tangible structures and forces.  
The player is a Programmer, working and navigating the paradigm space to fight for his / her boss.  The lanes extend from the Core (parent node), branching to two lanes. Each lane is guarded by a progression of Paradigm Nodes: the Procedural Gate at the farthest point (representing sequential execution and procedure calls), the Object Model in the middle (representing encapsulated objects with state and behavior), and two Functional Registers side-by-side protecting the Core entrance (representing pure function evaluation and immutability states). Inside each Core reside two Logic Shrines which must be resolved before the final “boss” can be accessed and defeated. The Paradigm Core (the boss) has two phases before being fully resolved, representing the transition from syntactic understanding (Phase 1: Syntax) to semantic mastery (Phase 2: Semantics), adding a twist to the bossfight, requiring both applied and theoretical programming paradigm knowledge.  
Cracking the enemy's Logic Shrines, defeating their Paradigm Core, and claiming the Paradigm Space as your own is the win condition; this means you have successfully proven yourself as a master of programming paradigms. Accumulating too many failures, losing all your nodes, and having your Paradigm Core corrupted will result in your loss condition.

For the characters, currently there will be 3 characters. The first is your mentor, Dynamic Dynamo, he is a computer scientist who’s spent his entire life working on solving complicated Logic Shrines and, in a tragic accident, lost his body to the Concurrency Overclocker. Now, in a robotic physique his genius managed to preserve, his goal is to guide and prevent you from making his same mistakes, ultimately helping you in surviving the Paradigm Space. Then, there are the bosses, eldritch deities of incomprehensible power, gods who are stuck in a theoretical space, unable to enter the real world; they are the Imperative Mother, and the Declarative King. The Imperative Mother will reward your gallantry, upon successfully defeating the Declarative King and bringing her to reality; she promises to grant you a wish. The Declarative King, likewise, aims to enter the real world, compelling you to destroy the Imperative Mother’s nodes, completing his ascension and rewarding you with the same obscure wish. Fighting for the Imperative Mother or Declarative King will result in the opposite being your boss, while mostly thematic, these characters will have their own distinct features based on their conceptual paradigms.

## **Glossary for 1.1** {#glossary-for-1.1}

**Player** \- The individual controlling the game. Takes on the role of a Programmer navigating the Paradigm Space to demonstrate mastery and hone the programming paradigms.

**Paradigm Space** \- An computational realm where the game takes place, representing a metaphysical reality where abstract computational ideas become tangible and interactive objects rather than ideas.

**Dynamic Dynamo** \- A renowned computer scientist who, suffering a tragic accident, lost his body to the Concurrency Overclocker. Now, he aims to guide future programmers, including you, into becoming the first to overcome the game.

**The Core** \- The final and most powerful structure on the Execution Path, it contains the essence of the Bosses. Once broken after two phases, their essence is released and actualized into the real world, finishing their ascension. Defeating the opposing side's core is the win condition for the game. 

- **Imperative Mother** \- One of the deities sealed inside their core, promising a wish in exchange for her ascension.  
- **Declarative King** \- Another deity sealed within their core, promising you power in exchange for serving him and liberating him from his core. 

**Paradigm Nodes** \- are the node structures that precede the Core, and impede your path towards it.

- Procedural Gate \- the 1st and farthest node in the Execution path. A guardian with the lowest hp out of the nodes.  
- Object Model \- the 2nd node. After defeating the procedural gate, the Object Model is the next obstacle, it features appendages representing object correlations and inheritance using diagrams, and has more hp than the procedural gate.  
- Functional Registers \- the 3rd node. After defeating the Object Model, you are one step closer to reaching the Core. The Functional Registers are the two pillars of nodes that protect the entrance to the Core and have higher hp than the Object Model.  
- Logic Shrines \- the 4th and last child of the Core. The Logic Shrines are unique in that they are close enough to the core for the boss to interfere with your attacks. In this node, there is a hidden extra challenge for the programmer to face.

**Consumables** \- These consumables, if available, can be taken during turns, which have their own respective buff.

## **1.2 Concepts Integration Strategy** {#1.2-concepts-integration-strategy}

**1.2.1 Character Logic and Programming Paradigm Correlations**

Deadlock's roster is built around characters whose abilities are small, readable metaphors for computing concepts, which is exactly what we need for teaching paradigms. Our plan is to cast selected characters as in-game “Mentors” whose ability fits the paradigm they represent, wherein they use their in-game abilities as interactive examples to how programming paradigms work. We intend to reuse that mapping across UI color-coding, transition animations, and flavor text. But for the most part, we decided to utilize just one “Mentor” or Character for this task, Dynamic Dynamo. If we manage to complete Dynamic Dynamo, then we intend to use other characters in Deadlock to add a wider range of character Mentors that can be responsible for providing tips for each CMSC 13 Concept.

These concepts include but are not limited to the following:

* Computer Paradigms

  * Declarative, Imperative, Flow Driven, Event Driven, Object Oriented, Aspect Oriented, Reflective, Array.

* Categories of programming languages

  * Machine, Assembly, High level, System, Scripting, Domain Specific, Visual, Esoteric Languages.

* Scripting vs System Languages

* Modularity and Separation of Concerns

* Mutability and Immutability

* Functional Programming

* Symbolic Computing

* Component Mapping between Programming Paradigms

* Object-Oriented Paradigm 

* Functional Paradigm s

* Logic Paradigms

**1.2.2 Thematic Integration**

	Our main game logic is a unique blend of Deadlock and Are You Smarter Than a 5th Grader. Our main environmental and ambient themes are inspired by deadlock but represent CMSC 13 related themes, we intend to bring out a blend of the uniqueness in the game’s design mechanics by representing it using the concepts we learn along the way in CMSC 13\.

**1.2.3 Gameplay Logic**

* Bosses \- The main plot points of the game. You choose a side, and must defeat the other boss and help your own boss ascend to gain your wish and win the game. Otherwise, if the other boss wins, then your boss fails to ascend resulting in your wish being revoked and losing the game.  
* Gameplay Loop  
  * Beginning \- You can either Start the game or continue off a saved game slot. By continuing, you resume the last state played by the specific slot you chose from. By starting a new game, a short skippable introduction to the game mechanics is introduced by picture slideshow or if reached, animation. Afterwards, the game's official mechanics begin.  
  * Gameplay \-  
    * You begin at the Procedural Gate, the furthermost Paradigm Node. By answering and solving the questions correctly, you begin to deal damage to the enemy side's nodes. Defeating a Paradigm Node will move you forward. You must defeat all the Paradigm Nodes to initiate the Boss Fight with the Core, which introduces you to the Boss, successfully defeating the Boss will result in the win condition.  
    * Progression Mechanic \- with each node destroyed, the questions get harder as you progress deeper and defeat more Paradigm Nodes, the Core will have the hardest questions, truly testing your paradigm ability both conceptually and in application.  
      * The Paradigm Nodes follow a progression:(Closest to Farthest, Easiest to Hardest)  
      * Procedural Gate \-\> Object Model \-\> Functional Registers \-\> Logic Shrines \-\> Core  
    * Choices \- determines whether you win or lose the neutral fighting spots.  
      * If an incorrect answer is given, a node of the allied Core will be damaged, if the next damage dealt reduces the node’s HP to 0, then it is destroyed.  
      * A correct answer will only deal a certain amount of damage to the opposing Core’s  nodes (which will be accounted for to reach 145 questions)  
    * Minimap \-  The minimap will serve as the “ladder” of the game. This will represent both sides’ current Paradigm Nodes. This will also be the player’s main reference for progress.  
    * Question Randomization \- Each Question will be randomized, and their respective choices are also going to be randomized. However, each question shall be categorized in difficulty.  
      * 70 multiple choice questions  
      * 75 programming questions. The programming questions shall be divided into 10|15|50.  
        * 50 questions must be about C or Java  
        * 10 questions shall be any language besides the aforementioned languages  
        * 15 questions shall be any language besides the aforementioned languages (including the one before this).  
  * Losing/Winning \- At the foremost,  a panel will be overlayed in front of the original gameplay panel. This will indicate whether or not you achieved Victory or Defeat. If we manage to reach it, we intend to play a sequence of slides, a short video,  or an animation for the victory and defeat cases, but this will only be implemented once the game is complete and there is still additional time, just to improve the game’s flair.  
* Additional Features  
  * Contact \[Mentor\] \- For now, will be replaced with Contact Dynamic Dynamo, as he is the only confirmed mentor. Dynamic Dynamo will provide a hint related to the question  
  * Abandon Question \- For the weak, choosing to give up a question will willingly surrender your turn, allowing your foremost Paradigm Node to be damaged and automatically getting the punishment of a wrongly answered question.  
  * Consumables \- There are currently 3 different consumables, these consumables will have a weighted function to randomize their drops, better consumables will be rarer than simpler consumables. These consumables are given randomly to help the Player.  
    * NullSlinger \- When used, nullifies one wrong choice from the choices. This is the most common consumable.  
    * Scripter’s Sacrifice \- When used, lets your turn deal twice as much damage than usual. However, using it more times than suggested will result in taking damage yourself. This means that the object has a set amount of uses and can be discarded afterwards, but by choosing not to discard it, it can still be used but every turn will damage the user once. This is currently the second rarest consumable.  
    * Refresher \- Resets the functional calls you can make to Dynamic Dynamo. Is currently the rarest consumable.

# **3\. Game Mechanics & Music Asset Mapping** {#3.-game-mechanics-&-music-asset-mapping}

## **3.1 How to Play Instructions** {#3.1-how-to-play-instructions}

| *Submission Instructions: Explain the exact rules of the game so that any player can instantly understand how to navigate your game. Describe the mouse interaction scheme, how lifelines are activated, scoring progression. Create a GUI for your How to PLay instructions (make sure that your instructions are clear).* |
| :---- |

	**3.1.1 Objective**

	The goal of this game is to “decode” or defeat the enemy’s parent node (the Core) by answering programming paradigm questions. Each correct answer damages the enemy’s Paradigm nodes. Likewise, a wrong answer will damage your nodes.

	**3.1.2 Setting**

	The game will take place inside a circuit board-esque map \- the Paradigm space. The fight will take place in a single lane (mimics an execution path). Each side has 5 defensive structures that must be destroyed in-order. 

| Order | Nodes | Health | Concepts asked |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 1 | Procedural gate | N/A | N/A |
| 2 | Object Model | N/A | N/A |
| 3 \- 4 | Functional Register | (N/A) \* 2 (both sides) | N/A |
| 5-6 | Logic Shrine | (N/A) \* 2 (both sides) | N/A |
| 7 | Paradigm Core (A Parent node) | (N/A) \* 2 (2 phase) | N/A |

Note: N/A for now since we still do not know most of the concepts’ “key details” that will be present in this course. Additionally, the damage has to be spread out to concern the entire list of questions, which, as we haven’t finished the complete set of questions, cannot yet be determined. The goal is to even out the problems to account for the health points of all the Paradigm Nodes including at least a couple instances of the Neutral Objectives. 

**3.1.3 Damage System**

- The correct answer deals N amount of damage to the enemy node.   
- Incorrect answer deals N amount of damage to your nodes.   
- Rift buff: deals additional damage ( N \+ x ) damage done passively by the Rift Function Decompiler in every turn until it expires.

**3.1.4 Questions and Multiple choices**

* Question type  
  * Multiple choices  
    * A,B,C,D  
  * Programming questions  
    * Code snippets  
    * Debugging  
    * Tracing

	**3.1.5 Mentors**

* **Dynamic dynamo \-** Provides a hint for the current problem (Limited to 3 uses at the start of the game).

	**3.1.6 Turn Structure**

1. If It’s your turn, Attack the foremost opposing node.  
2. Answer the questions  
3. If correctly Answered, Move forward by dealing damage. Else take damage instead.  
4. If the foremost node is broken, move forward to the next following node.  
5. Repeat;

	**3.1.6  Win/Lose condition**

	If either of the Cores is destroyed, the opposing side shall claim victory.

## **4.1 Java Implementation Approach** {#4.1-java-implementation-approach}

## **4.1.1 Implementation Approach**

We plan to build the GUI in Java Swing, following the same general architecture we used successfully in a previous Java game project (object-oriented panel/screen classes, an abstract GameState object which is a parent of all other objects, then for objects with multiple required instances, we will have their own distinct parent classes. We will also build upon that “old” architecture we learned from by implementing what we have learned from this course (and also using extra libraries we have not tried).

Note: These variable names are not final and will be adjusted as necessary.

* Question / Paradigm data: the 145 question objects (75 theoretical \+ 70 programming\~) will be modeled as a Question class (prompt, choices, correct index, paradigm tag, difficulty, hints) and loaded into paradigm-tagged collection (e.g., a Map\<Paradigm\> or List\<Question\>) so the game can access the appropriate node (current difficulty) question during runtime. 

  * For the questions class, we would prefer storing the data into one csv file so we can store it while still in the splash screen.

  * For the randomization of questions, our plan is to use a random function that chooses a question within a certain difficulty range (e.g. only easy questions shall appear randomly).

* Screens as classes: SplashScreen, MainMenu, RosterScreen, GameBoard, HowToPlay, WinScreen, LossScreen, CreditsScreen — each a JPanel swapped via a CardLayout on the main JFrame.

  * For the screens, it’s a pretty straight forward method of calling the selected overlay screen that will automatically put the game loop asleep.

* Window & resolution scaling: unlike our previous game, this project will account for window resizing from the start — using layout managers (GridBagLayout/relative constraints or other methods found in different libraries we have not used before) and scalable vector or by hiding resizable components while setting the program resolution to the monitor’s native resolution.

* Audio: We will create our own library to import assets, including audio, to trigger the effects mapped in Section 3.2. 

* Compiling and Executable \-  we will be using tools such as launch4j to convert our packages into both a Jar file and an executable file.
